source_read: Online-first PDF (Scand J Public Health, article pages 1–9 = PDF pp. 1–9), all pages read from the text layer; Tables I–III (PDF pp. 3–5) and Results checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Figures 1–2 (PDF p. 6) checked at 300 dpi

claims.note: The source says the toxicology register (Toxreg) did not hold the inventory's 151 hospital cases because they had no forensic examination. The 151 belong to the whole 1985–1996 inventory (Table I), while Toxreg only starts in 1994 and was compared with the 454 inventory deaths it could cover. The paper does not say how many of the 151 fall in 1994–1996, so '151' is the paper's own loose figure, not a 1994–1996 count. Toxreg also could not hold inventory deaths with a drug-use history but no positive toxicology (10% of the 1,061 forensic cases), and it only covers ages 10 to 60, except that deaths with both morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine enter at any age. (I added this heroin exception after step 2: my blind reading missed it.) The paper reports no autopsy rates.

anchors.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 3rd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Toxreg held 317 of the 454 inventory drug-related deaths. Inventory deaths with a recorded history of drug use but no positive toxicology cannot enter Toxreg: 10% of the 1,061 forensic cases. Toxreg did not hold the 151 hospital cases of the inventory because they had not been examined forensically (data not shown).

anchors.locator: Datasets › Swedish Toxreg dataset, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Toxreg takes every death from 1994 to 2012 whose forensic toxicology found an illegal drug, methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl, whatever the certified cause. Only deaths at ages 10 to 60 are included, except deaths with both morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine (a heroin marker), which enter at any age. Entry therefore needs a forensic examination with positive toxicology.
The inventory covers 1985–1996: 1,061 forensic cases plus 151 hospital cases, 1,212 in total. Toxreg covers 1994–2012, so the 151 hospital cases span a longer period than the Toxreg comparison.

claims.overstatement: The claim describes the toxicology register as taking 'any death' with a listed drug found at forensic examination. Toxreg only includes deaths at ages 10 to 60, except deaths with both morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine (heroin), which enter at any age (PDF p. 3). The certificate selection has no age limit (PDF p. 8), so part of the 3,259 certificate-only deaths are outside Toxreg's range by design. The claim should mention the age limit. (I added the heroin exception after step 2: my blind reading missed it.) Table III, the source of 96% and 23%, gives no period. Its Toxreg column sums to 5,831, which matches the 1997–2012 annual values in Figure 1 rather than the 1994–2012 total of 6,448 (editors' check), so the figures should not be tied to 1994–2012.
claims.note: All numbers match: 4,238, 2,210, 3,259 and 9,707 are printed in Figure 2 (PDF p. 6). The text's 34% and 43% recompute as 2,210/6,448 = 34.3% and 3,259/7,497 = 43.5%. 788/819 = 96.2% and 158/700 = 22.6%. The Toxreg total is 6,448 in Figure 2 but 6,648 in Table I. The cross-country point is the authors' conclusion from one country's data; the claim says so.

anchors.extracted: The Swedish specification (official yearbook 1987–2014) counts both underlying and contributory causes. The EMCDDA specification counts underlying causes only. The US NIDA specification also uses underlying causes only and is narrower still: poisonings only, no dependence.

anchors.locator: Datasets › Three NMR selections, 2nd paragraph (starts on p. 2; the 'anywhere on the certificate' sentence is on p. 3); Table II (PDF p. 4)
anchors.extracted: In the Swedish specification a death counts if a drug-related condition appears anywhere on the certificate. NMR/EMCDDA requires a drug-related underlying cause. In Table II, the EMCDDA column marks 'No' for several codes the Swedish list includes: ICD-9 292, 304.1, 305.2–305.9; ICD-10 F13, F18, O35.5, P04.4, both T40.4 rows, Z50.3, Z71.5 and Z72.2.

Toxreg takes all deaths from 1994 to 2012 whose forensic toxicology showed an illegal drug, methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl, whether or not the death was certified as drug-related. Each death is listed once, under a main drug chosen by a priority order. Only ages 10 to 60 are included, except deaths with both morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine, which enter at any age.

anchors.locator: Figure 2 (Venn diagram, 1994–2012); text on PDF p. 5, Data description, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Toxreg N = 6,448; NMR/Sweden N = 7,497; 4,238 in both; 2,210 in Toxreg only; 3,259 in NMR/Sweden only; 9,707 in either. The text says 34% of Toxreg deaths are not in NMR/Sweden and 43% of NMR/Sweden deaths are not in Toxreg. Table I gives Toxreg N = 6,648 instead.

anchors.locator: Table III, Heroin and THC rows (NMR/Sweden columns)
anchors.extracted: Main drug heroin: 819 in Toxreg, 788 (96%) also in NMR/Sweden and 740 (90%) in NMR/EMCDDA. THC: 700 in Toxreg, 158 (23%) in NMR/Sweden and 61 (9%) in NMR/EMCDDA. No period is stated.

International comparability depends on how deaths are investigated and certified, especially the rate of forensic investigation. Comparing numbers or rates between countries would mislead; comparing trends is meaningful if no major change in investigation or certification practice has occurred. The study analysed only Swedish data.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Pros and cons of statistics based on NMRs and forensic toxicology, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Toxicology-based statistics can be ready months after death, before any further investigation, physician's certification or ICD coding. The death certificate is mandatory at every death in Sweden (PDF p. 2). Certification is by a physician.

claims.note: All numbers match the printed page: 761, 63%, 1,212, 1,061, 151, 28% (under a third), 419, 30, 1,181 (Table I), 317, 454 and 43. 'About a third differed in each direction' recomputes as 451/1,212 = 37.2% of inventory deaths not in the selection and 419/1,181 = 35.5% of selection deaths not in the inventory. The matching itself gives 761 + 419 = 1,180, against Table I's 1,181. Of the 389 selection deaths outside the inventory definition, only 56 are described (49 drownings after medicines or alcohol- or medicine-related, 7 with no cause found); the claim's 'including' is accurate. Of the 30 inventory misses, 21 were Stockholm residents who died elsewhere and 9 were administrative misses, so the inventory was itself incomplete. The authors' 'one-quarter' missing from Toxreg (PDF p. 7) does not match 137/454 = 30.2%.

anchors.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 761 (63%) of the 1,212 inventory deaths were in NMR/Stockholm, and 734 (69%) of the 1,061 forensic cases. By main drug, heroin was highest (80%) and cocaine lowest (13%); 81% of injection deaths were captured. The paper reports 'sensitivity' 64.5% (61.7–67.2) and 'PPV' 62.8% (60.4–65.1). But 62.8% = 761/1,212 and 64.5% ≈ 761/1,180, so the two labels appear swapped relative to their usual meaning (editors' arithmetic).

anchors.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: 419 NMR/Stockholm deaths were not in the inventory. Judged from their certificates, 30 were confirmed drug-related deaths: 21 Stockholm residents who died elsewhere and 9 missed for administrative reasons. Of the rest, 49 were suicidal bathtub drownings after taking medicines or were related to alcohol or medicines rather than illegal drugs, and 7 had no cause found. Only 28% of the 151 hospital deaths (mainly HIV-positive people) were in NMR/Stockholm.

anchors.locator: Datasets › Inventory of DRDs in the Stockholm area (1985–1996), 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Each inventory death was assessed individually. The inventory took all decedents with a personal history of drug use problems or illegal drugs present at death. It counted deaths involving illegal drugs or non-prescribed morphine or methadone, and deaths of anyone with such a history whatever the cause; deaths from prescribed methadone or morphine were excluded. It is therefore not a count of poisonings.

anchors.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 3rd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Toxreg held 317 of 454 inventory deaths. 43 Toxreg cases were not inventory deaths because the forensic findings pointed to medical treatment (mostly opioid medicines), not illicit use. The paper's 'sensitivity' of 88.1% equals 317/360, so the 43 are in addition to the 317, although the text says 'of the 317'. Its CI is printed as 84.3–81.2. Its 'PPV' of 69.8% equals 317/454.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Main results; Pros and cons of statistics based on NMRs and forensic toxicology, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: About one-third of inventory cases were not captured by the certificate-based data, and about one-quarter were missing from the toxicology-based data. Both included about as many deaths unrelated to drug use. One-third of certificates for inventory deaths did not mention drugs. ICD codes do not separate illegal from other drugs, and T40.4 groups dissimilar drugs.

The inventory is 20 years old, so later data could not be validated. The datasets captured acute poisonings far better than chronic drug-related conditions, so recent coverage of all drug mortality may be lower.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Most useful statistics for international comparisons, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: By the inventory, only about two-thirds of the deaths in the certificate selection were related to drug use. Totals are roughly right, but the selection is a questionable basis for detailed analyses.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed: Table III's Toxreg column sums to 5,831 and its NMR/EMCDDA column to 2,840. 2,991/5,831 = 51.3% and 3,608/6,448 = 56.0%.

risk_of_bias.note: I agree with JBI-prevalence, overall high. The raw linkage counts (Figure 2, Table III) carry less risk than the validation statistics. The 'missed' share depends on an unvalidated, author-built reference that counts deaths of people with a history of drug use whatever the cause, and that reference was assessed unblinded. The printed accuracy statistics are mislabelled. QUADAS-2-style domains (reference standard, flow and timing) would reach the same judgment.

interpretation_gap.note: I agree with 'substantial'. The title's 'one-third' needs the inventory's broad definition and the 1985–1996 Stockholm setting. The claim that toxicology statistics were 'more complete' compares 3 years with 12. 'DRDs due to poisoning were captured well' has no figure behind it. The trend conclusion rests on inspection by eye, while the ratios between the series changed.

missed: Period mismatch in the Toxreg paragraph (PDF p. 5, right column; Table I). The 151 hospital deaths and the 10% of the 1,061 forensic cases without positive toxicology refer to the whole 1985–1996 inventory, but Toxreg was compared only with the 454 inventory deaths of 1994–1996. How many hospital deaths, or forensic cases without positive toxicology, fall in 1994–1996 is not given, and Toxreg's 137 missed deaths are never broken down. KF4 and the claim text repeat '151' as if it applied to the 1994–1996 comparison.

The Discussion suggests that frequent forensic examination may partly explain why Nordic and Baltic countries have higher drug-death rates than most other European countries (PDF p. 8, Most useful statistics…, 2nd paragraph). This is untested in the study, which analysed only Swedish data, and is relevant to the cross-country wording in the claims.
